meanings.short: The state of a system with the lowest possible energy.
meanings.long: A quantum system cannot have less energy than its ground state. For a particle in a well the ground-state wavefunction has no nodes, and even it keeps some energy, the zero-point energy.

meanings.short: Any state of a system with more energy than its lowest state.
meanings.long: The first excited state is the next level up from the ground state; in a one-dimensional well it has exactly one node. A system in an excited state can drop to a lower one, giving the difference away, for instance as a photon.

meanings.short: Of a matrix or operator: equal to its own conjugate transpose, which makes all its eigenvalues real numbers.
meanings.long: An operator Q is Hermitian when moving it from one side of an inner product to the other changes nothing: (Ψ₁, QΨ₂) = (QΨ₁, Ψ₂). Its eigenvalues are real and its eigenfunctions can be chosen orthonormal, which is why quantum mechanics uses Hermitian operators for everything that can be measured.

meanings.short: The partner of an operator that does the same job from the other side of an inner product; for a matrix, its conjugate transpose.
meanings.long: The Hermitian conjugate Q† of an operator Q is defined by (Ψ₁, QΨ₂) = (Q†Ψ₁, Ψ₂) for all wavefunctions. For a matrix it means swapping rows and columns and taking the complex conjugate of every entry. An operator equal to its Hermitian conjugate is Hermitian.

meanings.short: The average result expected from many measurements of a quantity, each made on an identically prepared system.
meanings.long: For values Q₁, Q₂, … found with probabilities p₁, p₂, …, the expectation value is the sum of each value times its probability. In quantum mechanics it is written ⟨Q⟩ and found from the wavefunction as the integral of Ψ* QΨ. It need not be a value any single measurement can give.

meanings.short: A measure of spread: the average of the squared distance of each value from the mean.
meanings.long: The variance of a quantity Q is ⟨(Q − ⟨Q⟩)²⟩, which equals ⟨Q²⟩ − ⟨Q⟩². It is never negative, and zero only when Q always takes one value. Its square root is the standard deviation.

meanings.short: A measure of how widely values are spread around their average, in the same units as the values: the square root of the variance.
meanings.long: For a bell-shaped (Gaussian) spread, about two thirds of the values lie within one standard deviation of the mean. Physicists often write it σ, or ΔQ when it is the uncertainty of a quantum measurement.

everyday: Not doubt or ignorance about a value: in quantum mechanics it is the spread of results that a perfectly made measurement still gives.

meanings.short: In quantum mechanics: the spread of the results that repeated measurements of a quantity give on identically prepared systems.
meanings.long: The uncertainty ΔQ of an operator Q in a state Ψ is the standard deviation of its results: (ΔQ)² = ⟨Q²⟩ − ⟨Q⟩². It is zero exactly when Ψ is an eigenstate of Q, so that every measurement gives the same value.

meanings.short: A family of standard patterns on the surface of a sphere, labelled l and m, from which any pattern on a sphere can be built.
meanings.long: The spherical harmonics Y_lm(θ, φ) are the functions of direction that have definite angular momentum: they are the shared eigenfunctions of L² and L_z. They are made from associated Legendre functions of θ times e^(imφ), and they play the role on a sphere that sines and cosines play on a line.

meanings.short: A standard family of polynomials P₀, P₁, P₂, … in cos θ that describe how a quantity varies with angle around an axis.
meanings.long: P_l has degree l and solves Legendre's equation; P₀ = 1, P₁ = x, P₂ = (3x² − 1)/2 with x = cos θ. They are orthogonal on −1 ≤ x ≤ 1 and are even or odd as l is even or odd. Up to a constant factor, they are the spherical harmonics with m = 0.

meanings.short: Relatives of the Legendre polynomials, labelled by two whole numbers l and m, that give the angle θ part of the spherical harmonics.
meanings.long: They solve the equation that results when the angular-momentum eigenvalue equation is separated, with the φ dependence e^(imφ) removed. For m = 0 they reduce to the Legendre polynomials; for other m they are found by differentiating P_l |m| times and multiplying by (1 − x²)^(|m|/2).

meanings.short: A differential equation in x = cos θ whose well-behaved solutions are the Legendre polynomials.
meanings.long: It is (1 − x²)P'' − 2xP' + l(l + 1)P = 0. Its solutions stay finite at both poles, x = ±1, only when l is a whole number, and then they are the polynomials P_l.

meanings.short: A standard family of polynomials that, multiplied by a bell-shaped factor, give the energy states of the quantum harmonic oscillator.
meanings.long: The nth oscillator state is H_n(u) e^(−u²/2), with u the position in natural units. H_n has degree n, is even or odd as n is, and has n real zeros, which become the n nodes of the state.

meanings.short: A potential energy that depends only on the distance from a centre, not on direction, such as gravity or the electric pull of a nucleus.
meanings.long: A central potential V(r) is spherically symmetric, so angular momentum is conserved. In quantum mechanics this lets the wavefunction be split into a radial part times a spherical harmonic.

meanings.short: The real potential plus a term for the angular motion, which turns a problem in three dimensions into one along the radius.
meanings.long: For a body of mass m with angular momentum L in a central potential V(r), the radial motion feels V(r) + L²/(2mr²); in quantum mechanics L² becomes ħ²l(l + 1). The added centrifugal term is repulsive and keeps bodies with angular momentum away from the centre.

meanings.short: The equation for how a quantity depends on distance from a centre, left over once the dependence on direction has been dealt with.
meanings.long: For an orbit it is the equation of motion for the distance r, with angular momentum entering as an extra term; for a field it is the part of Laplace's or Poisson's equation in r. Separating off the directions turns a problem in three dimensions into one along a line.

meanings.short: The equation for how a wavefunction changes with distance from the centre, left over once the dependence on direction has been separated off.
meanings.long: In a central potential the wavefunction is R(r) Y_lm(θ, φ). Writing R = u/r turns the Schrödinger equation into a one-dimensional equation for u(r) with an effective potential, the radial equation.

meanings.short: Newton's second law written for the direction along the radius, pointing in or out from the centre of the circle or sphere.
meanings.long: It sets the net force along the radius equal to mass times the radial acceleration. For circular motion this acceleration points towards the centre.

meanings.short: The single mass that turns a two-body problem into one body moving about a fixed centre: the product of the masses over their sum.
meanings.long: For masses m₁ and m₂ the reduced mass is μ = m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂), smaller than either. In hydrogen the proton is so much heavier that μ is very nearly the electron mass, but the small difference shows up in precise spectra.

meanings.short: An amount added to the phase of a wave, which moves its crests forward or back without changing its shape.
meanings.long: Multiplying a wave by e^(iδ) shifts its phase by δ. A piece of glass in one arm of an interferometer, or a reflection, can shift the phase and so change where the waves add or cancel.

meanings.short: In scattering: the extra phase that the outgoing wave carries because of the potential, compared with the same wave with no potential.
meanings.long: Far from the potential the outgoing wave is the free one with its phase moved by δ. The phase shift holds all the information about the scattering: the probability of scattering goes as sin²δ, and the rate at which δ changes with energy gives the time delay of a wave packet.

meanings.short: The number that says how strongly a wave is scattered by a target; its squared size gives the probability of scattering.
meanings.long: The outgoing wave is the unscattered wave plus a scattered wave whose size is the scattering amplitude. In one dimension it is e^(iδ) sin δ in terms of the phase shift; in three dimensions it depends on the direction, and its square gives the cross-section.

meanings.short: The idea that, in a sum of many waves, only those whose phase hardly changes from one to the next add up; the rest cancel.
meanings.long: When an integral over k has a rapidly changing phase, neighbouring contributions cancel except where the phase is stationary, that is where its derivative is zero. Applied to a wave packet, this shows that the peak moves at the group velocity dω/dk.

everyday: Stationary does not mean the particle is at rest: the wavefunction still turns in phase, but nothing measurable changes.

meanings.short: A quantum state of definite energy, whose wavefunction changes in time only by a turning phase, so its measurable properties never change.
meanings.long: A stationary state has the form Ψ(x, t) = e^(−iEt/ħ) ψ(x), where ψ solves the time-independent Schrödinger equation with energy E. Expectation values in it are the same at all times; a sum of stationary states with different energies is not stationary.

meanings.short: The equation that gives the states of definite energy of a quantum system, and those energies, with time left out.
meanings.long: It reads Hψ = Eψ: the Hamiltonian acting on ψ gives the energy E times ψ. It is an eigenvalue equation, and for bound states only certain energies have well-behaved solutions, which is why energy is quantized.

meanings.short: Probability per unit length, area or volume: multiplied by a small interval, it gives the chance that the value falls there.
meanings.long: A probability density p(x) is never negative and its integral over all values is 1. The chance of finding x between a and b is the integral of p from a to b. In quantum mechanics |Ψ(x)|² is the probability density for finding the particle at x.

meanings.short: The rate at which the probability of finding a particle flows past a point, just as electric current is the flow of charge.
meanings.long: In one dimension it is J = (ħ/2mi)(Ψ*Ψ' − ΨΨ*'). Together with the probability density it obeys a conservation law: the probability in a region changes only by what flows in or out. Ratios of currents give the reflection and transmission coefficients.

meanings.short: Of a function, usually a wavefunction: having a finite total of |Ψ|² over all space, so it can be scaled to give total probability one.
meanings.long: A wavefunction is normalizable, or square-integrable, when the integral of |Ψ|² is finite. Dividing by the square root of that integral normalizes it. Bound states are normalizable; plane waves and scattering states are not, and describe a particle only when superposed into packets.

meanings.short: The rule that the total probability of finding a particle somewhere stays equal to one as time passes.
meanings.long: The Schrödinger equation keeps the integral of |Ψ|² constant because the Hamiltonian is Hermitian. Locally the same fact says that probability only moves from place to place, carried by the probability current.

meanings.short: In quantum physics, an operator that adds one quantum of energy, or one particle, to a state; also called a raising operator.
meanings.long: For the harmonic oscillator the creation operator a† turns the state with N quanta into the one with N + 1, raising the energy by ħω. Starting from the ground state, repeated use of a† builds every higher state.

meanings.short: An angular-momentum raising operator: it turns a state with component m along an axis into one with m + 1.
An operator that counts: its eigenvalues are 0, 1, 2, …, the number of quanta (or particles) in a state.
meanings.long: For the harmonic oscillator it is N = a†a, the creation operator times the annihilation operator. It is Hermitian, and the Hamiltonian is ħω(N + ½), so counting quanta gives the energy.

meanings.short: Three particular two-by-two matrices, σ₁, σ₂ and σ₃ (or σx, σy, σz), that describe the spin of an electron and do not commute.
meanings.long: Each Pauli matrix is Hermitian, squares to the identity and has eigenvalues +1 and −1. Multiplied by ħ/2 they are the operators for the three components of spin one half; their commutators, such as [σx, σy] = 2iσz, are the algebra of angular momentum.

meanings.short: In quantum mechanics, the rule that turns a wavefunction into the information about momentum: take the slope and multiply by ħ/i.
meanings.long: In position space the momentum operator is p = (ħ/i) d/dx. A wave e^(ikx) is its eigenstate with momentum ħk. With the position operator it obeys [x, p] = iħ, the root of the uncertainty principle.

meanings.short: In quantum mechanics, the operator for position: it multiplies a wavefunction by x.
meanings.long: The position operator x̂ acts by x̂f(x) = xf(x). It does not commute with the momentum operator: xp − px = iħ.

meanings.short: The total energy of a system written in terms of its positions and momenta; in quantum mechanics, the operator for energy.
meanings.long: Classically the Hamiltonian H(q, p) is usually the kinetic plus the potential energy, and Hamilton's equations give the motion from it. In quantum mechanics the Hamiltonian is the energy operator, for example −(ħ²/2m) d²/dx² + V(x), and it drives the Schrödinger equation.

meanings.short: A state in which a quantity has one definite value: the operator for that quantity only multiplies the state by a number.
meanings.long: If QΨ = qΨ, then Ψ is an eigenstate of Q with eigenvalue q, and measuring Q in that state gives q every time. An energy eigenstate is a stationary state.

meanings.short: A function that an operator changes only by multiplying it by a number, the eigenvalue: the function version of an eigenvector.
meanings.long: e^(kx) is an eigenfunction of d/dx with eigenvalue k; sin(nx) is an eigenfunction of d²/dx² with eigenvalue −n². In quantum mechanics the eigenfunctions of a Hermitian operator are the states with a definite value of its quantity.

meanings.short: A whole number, or a whole number plus a half, that labels one of the allowed states of a quantum system.
meanings.long: A quantum state is often named by a few quantum numbers, one for each quantity that has a definite value in it. The hydrogen states are labelled n, l and m: energy, size of the angular momentum, and its component along an axis.

meanings.short: The whole number n = 1, 2, 3, … that fixes the energy of a state of the hydrogen atom.
meanings.long: In hydrogen n equals the number of nodes of the radial function plus l plus 1, and the energy is −13.6 eV divided by n². For each n the angular momentum number l runs from 0 to n − 1, so all those states share one energy.

meanings.short: The natural size of a hydrogen atom, about 0.053 nanometres (0.529 ångström).
meanings.long: The Bohr radius a₀ = ħ²/(me²) comes from balancing the electron's typical kinetic energy against its electric potential energy. It is the most likely distance of the electron from the proton in the ground state of hydrogen.

meanings.short: A pure number, about 1/137, that measures the strength of the electric force between charged particles.
meanings.long: It is α = e²/(ħc) in Gaussian units (e²/(4πε₀ħc) in SI). Because it has no units it is the same in every system of units; the electron in hydrogen moves at about α times the speed of light.

meanings.short: A length fixed by a particle's mass, h divided by mass times the speed of light; for the electron, about 2.4 picometres.
meanings.long: The Compton wavelength h/(mc) sets the shift in wavelength when light scatters off a particle of mass m. It is also roughly the distance below which a particle cannot be located without enough energy to create new particles.

meanings.short: A length of about 2.8 femtometres built from the electron's charge and mass; it is not the electron's actual size.
meanings.long: It is e²/(mc²), the radius at which the electric energy of a ball of charge would be about equal to the electron's rest energy. It sets the size of the cross-section for Thomson scattering.

meanings.short: The scattering of light by a free electron as classical physics describes it, with no change in the light's wavelength.
meanings.long: The light's electric field shakes the electron, which radiates at the same frequency in new directions. It is the low-energy limit of Compton scattering; at higher energies the measured wavelength shift shows that light comes in photons.

meanings.short: The least energy needed to pull one electron out of the surface of a particular metal.
meanings.long: In the photoelectric effect a photon of energy hν frees an electron only if hν is at least the work function W, and the fastest electrons leave with kinetic energy hν − W. It is typically a few electronvolts.

meanings.short: The lowest frequency of light that can knock electrons out of a metal, however bright the light is.
meanings.long: It is the work function divided by Planck's constant, ν₀ = W/h. Below it no photoelectric current flows; classical wave theory could not explain why there is such a threshold.

meanings.short: The basic constant of quantum physics, about 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ joule seconds, linking a photon's energy to its frequency.
meanings.long: A photon of frequency ν has energy E = hν. The reduced constant ħ = h/2π, about 1.05 × 10⁻³⁴ joule seconds, is used with angular frequency, E = ħω. Its units, energy times time, are those of angular momentum, and it sets the scale at which quantum effects matter.

meanings.short: The rules that give every particle a wave: its momentum fixes the wavelength and its energy fixes the frequency.
meanings.long: They read p = ħk and E = ħω, so the wavelength is λ = h/p. De Broglie proposed them for electrons in 1924, extending to matter what Einstein had found for light.

meanings.short: The wavelength of the wave that quantum mechanics links to a moving particle: Planck's constant divided by its momentum.
meanings.long: λ = h/p. It is tiny for everyday objects, which is why they behave classically, but comparable to atomic sizes for slow electrons, which then diffract like waves.

meanings.short: The wave that quantum mechanics links to a particle such as an electron, which can interfere and diffract like light.
meanings.long: De Broglie's matter wave became the wavefunction of the Schrödinger equation. Its value at a point cannot be measured directly; only |Ψ|², a probability density, and the patterns it makes can be observed.

meanings.short: A link between two or more particles whose joint state cannot be split into a separate state for each, so measurements on them are correlated.
meanings.long: A state of two particles is entangled when it cannot be written as (a state of particle 1) times (a state of particle 2). Measuring one particle then tells you about the other, however far apart they are, although this cannot be used to send a signal.

meanings.short: The sudden change of a quantum state, at a measurement, into the state that matches the result found.
meanings.long: After a measurement of Q gives the eigenvalue q, the state is the matching eigenstate, so an immediate second measurement gives q again. The collapse is a rule of the theory added to the Schrödinger equation; what it means physically is still debated.

meanings.short: The rule of quantum mechanics that says what a measurement can give, with what probability, and what state it leaves.
meanings.long: Measuring a Hermitian operator gives one of its eigenvalues. Writing the state as a sum of eigenstates with coefficients αᵢ, the result qᵢ comes with probability |αᵢ|², and afterwards the system is in that eigenstate.

meanings.short: A measurement that learns something about an object from a particle that never touched it, using quantum interference.
meanings.long: In the Elitzur–Vaidman bomb test, a photon that reaches a detector which interference would otherwise keep dark proves that a working bomb blocks the other path, although that photon took the path without the bomb. No photon needs to touch the bomb for the test to find a working one, though the bomb explodes in some runs.

meanings.short: A device, such as a half-silvered mirror, that lets part of a beam of light through and reflects the rest.
meanings.long: A balanced beam splitter reflects and transmits with equal probability. For a single photon it does not split the photon but puts it into a superposition of the two outgoing paths.

meanings.short: An instrument that splits light into two paths with one beam splitter and joins them at a second, so the paths interfere.
meanings.long: Whether light leaves by one exit or the other depends on the phase difference between the two paths. Sent one photon at a time, it shows that each photon travels both paths in superposition.

meanings.short: The sharp peak in scattering probability against energy near a resonance, fixed by the resonance's energy and its width.
meanings.long: Near a resonant energy E_α the probability goes as (Γ/2)² / ((E − E_α)² + (Γ/2)²): it reaches its peak at E_α and falls to half at E_α ± Γ/2. The width Γ is ħ divided by the lifetime of the trapped state. Mathematically it is a Lorentzian.

meanings.short: A rule that counts the bound states of a potential from how much its scattering phase shift changes between zero and very high energy.
meanings.long: The number of bound states is N_b = (δ(0) − δ(∞))/π. It links two different kinds of state: the trapped bound states and the scattering states that pass by.

meanings.short: The complete passing of a particle over a well or through a barrier at special energies, where its waves fit the region exactly.
meanings.long: For a square well, transmission is perfect when a whole number of half wavelengths fits across the well: then the waves reflected at the two edges cancel. The energies match the levels of an infinitely deep well of the same width.

meanings.short: The width of a peak measured at half its greatest height: a standard way to say how sharp a peak is.
meanings.long: For the Breit–Wigner peak it is the width Γ: the curve falls to half its maximum at E_α − Γ/2 and E_α + Γ/2. A narrow width means a long-lived resonance.

meanings.short: A state in which a particle stays trapped near a potential, such as an electron held in an atom.
meanings.long: In quantum mechanics a bound state is a normalizable energy eigenstate: its wavefunction dies away far from the potential. Bound-state energies are quantized, unlike the continuous energies of particles that come in and leave.

meanings.short: A state of definite energy that describes a particle coming in from far away and leaving again, rather than staying trapped.
meanings.long: Scattering states extend to infinity, so they cannot be normalized; superposing them builds wave packets that describe a particle being scattered. Their energies form a continuous range.

meanings.short: The fraction of particles (or of a wave's energy) that passes through a barrier, step or boundary.
meanings.long: In quantum mechanics it is the transmitted probability current divided by the incoming current. With the reflection coefficient it adds up to one, because probability is conserved.

meanings.short: At a boundary between two media: the transmitted wave's amplitude divided by the incoming wave's amplitude; it can be larger than one.
The fraction of particles (or of a wave's energy) that bounces back from a barrier, step or boundary.
meanings.long: In quantum mechanics it is the reflected probability current divided by the incoming current, R = J_reflected/J_incoming, and R + T = 1. Unlike a classical particle, a quantum one can be reflected even when it has enough energy to pass.

meanings.short: At a boundary between two media: the reflected wave's amplitude divided by the incoming wave's amplitude; negative when the reflected wave is turned upside down.
Of a region: where a particle's energy is less than the potential energy, so classical physics says it can never be there.
meanings.long: In such a region the kinetic energy would be negative. A quantum wavefunction does not vanish there but decays, bending away from the axis, which allows tunnelling through thin barriers.

meanings.short: Of a region: where a particle's energy is more than the potential energy, so classical physics lets it move there.
meanings.long: There the kinetic energy is positive and the quantum wavefunction bends towards the axis, oscillating like a sine wave with a local de Broglie wavelength. Where the energy only just exceeds the potential the wave is long and large, as a classical particle moves slowly there.

meanings.short: A way of finding approximate quantum results from classical ideas, valid when the potential changes little over one wavelength.
meanings.long: Where the potential varies slowly the wavefunction looks locally like a wave with a de Broglie wavelength set by the local momentum, and its size is largest where a classical particle moves slowly. The WKB method is its systematic form.

meanings.short: The idea that quantum mechanics must agree with classical physics in the limit where quantum effects become small, such as for large quantum numbers.
meanings.long: For a highly excited state, the quantum probability of finding a particle in a region, averaged over the fast wiggles, approaches the fraction of time a classical particle spends there. Bohr used the idea to guide early quantum theory.

meanings.short: The rule that the bound states of a one-dimensional potential, listed by energy, have 0, 1, 2, … nodes.
meanings.long: The nth bound state has n − 1 nodes, points inside where the wavefunction crosses zero; so the ground state has none. The 8.04 lesson proves it for a potential that grows without limit far away, but it holds for the bound states of any reasonable one-dimensional potential.

meanings.short: A numerical way to find allowed energies: start at one end, step across, and adjust the energy until the solution behaves at the other end.
meanings.long: At a wrong energy the solution of the Schrödinger equation runs off to plus or minus infinity; the allowed energies lie where it switches from one to the other. Trying energies and narrowing the gap, like adjusting a gun's aim, homes in on each bound state.

meanings.short: A potential energy that is lower by a fixed amount inside an interval and constant outside it, shaped like a box with straight walls.
meanings.long: In an infinite square well the walls are infinitely high and the particle is trapped in a box, with energies proportional to n². A finite well has a fixed depth: it always holds at least one bound state, and particles with enough energy pass over it.

origin: Latin degenerare, to depart from its kind.
everyday: Nothing to do with moral decline: in physics it is about different states sharing the same value.

meanings.short: The sharing of one energy by several different quantum states, or the number of states that share it.
meanings.long: A level is g-fold degenerate when g independent states have its energy, and g is then its degeneracy. In hydrogen level n has degeneracy n² (without spin); in one dimension bound states have no degeneracy at all.

meanings.short: In fitting data: the fact that two quantities can change together without changing what is observed, so the data cannot tell them apart.
meanings.long: In galaxy dynamics the mass profile and the shapes of the stars' orbits can fit the same velocity measurements (the mass–anisotropy degeneracy); in stellar populations an older age can look like a higher metallicity. Data of another kind is needed to break it.

meanings.short: Of electrons or neutrons packed very densely: the filling of every low energy level, whose resistance to further squeezing holds up a star.
meanings.long: Fermions cannot share a state, so squeezing them forces them into higher levels, which costs energy even at zero temperature. That pressure, not heat, supports white dwarfs and neutron stars.

meanings.short: Of an operator: having two or more independent eigenvectors with the same eigenvalue.
Whether a function or state stays the same (even) or changes sign (odd) when every position is reflected through the origin.
meanings.long: An even function has f(−x) = f(x), an odd one f(−x) = −f(x). In an even potential the energy eigenstates can be chosen with definite parity; the Legendre polynomial P_l has parity (−1)^l.

meanings.short: Of a rearrangement of a list: whether it can be made from an even or an odd number of swaps of two items.
An operator that commutes with every member of a family of related operators, such as L², which commutes with all three components of angular momentum.
meanings.long: Because it commutes with them all, it can share eigenstates with any one of them. That is why states can be labelled at once by L² and L_z, giving the quantum numbers l and m.

meanings.short: The rule that a function and its Fourier transform have the same total of squared size, so no probability is lost in changing description.
meanings.long: In quantum mechanics it says that the integral of |Ψ(x)|² over x equals the integral of |Φ(p)|² over p, so a wavefunction normalized in position space is normalized in momentum space too. The general version is Plancherel's theorem.

meanings.short: A way of describing a quantum state by how likely each momentum is, instead of each position.
meanings.long: The momentum-space wavefunction Φ(p) is the Fourier transform of the position-space wavefunction Ψ(x); |Φ(p)|² is the probability density for momentum. The two descriptions hold the same information.

meanings.short: The bell-shaped curve e to the minus x squared, or a quantity spread out with that shape; also called a normal distribution.
meanings.long: A Gaussian with mean μ and standard deviation σ is proportional to e^(−(x − μ)²/(2σ²)). It describes random errors, each velocity component of the molecules in a gas, and the least-uncertain quantum wave packets; the central limit theorem explains why it is so common.

meanings.short: A system of units for electricity in which Coulomb's law has no 4πε₀, so formulas such as e²/r look simpler than in SI units.
meanings.long: Charge is measured so that the force between two charges is just q₁q₂/r². Many physics texts, including the MIT quantum notes, use it; to convert a formula to SI, replace e² by e²/(4πε₀).

meanings.short: A filter that lets through only light whose electric field points along one direction and blocks light polarized at right angles to it.
meanings.long: Light polarized at angle θ to the filter's axis passes with intensity cos²θ times the original (Malus's law). For single photons that factor is the probability that each photon gets through: an early example of quantum probability.

meanings.short: A particle of light: the smallest amount of energy that light of a given frequency can carry.
meanings.long: A photon of frequency ν has energy hν and momentum h/λ, and no mass. Light behaves as a wave when it spreads and interferes, and as photons when it is emitted or absorbed, as in the photoelectric effect.

everyday: Not a device or an official that controls something: a temporary change to a problem that makes a calculation possible.

meanings.short: A temporary change to a problem, such as a far-away wall, that makes a calculation finite, removed at the end of the calculation.
meanings.long: To count the scattering states in the proof of Levinson's theorem a second wall is placed far away, which turns them into countable bound states of a wide well. Its effect fades as the wall is moved off to infinity.

meanings.short: Of a set of functions: enough of them that any reasonable function can be written as a sum of them.
meanings.long: The eigenfunctions of a Hermitian operator are complete, so any wavefunction is a sum of eigenfunctions with suitable coefficients, as any periodic function is a sum of sines and cosines. Completeness is what lets the measurement postulate give a probability to every eigenvalue.
